Sabbath
SAB-uth
noun (biblical theology / fourth commandment / Lord's Day)
Hebrew shabbat (“rest, cessation”), from the verb shabat (to rest, to cease from labor); into Greek sabbaton (σάββατον) and Latin sabbatum; entered English via Old French sabbat; the creation rest of God (Gen 2:2–3) precedes and grounds the Mosaic legislation (Exod 20:8–11); the New Testament's transfer of Sabbath observance to the first day of the week (the Lord's Day) is the Reformed position, grounded in the resurrection and the apostolic practice of Sunday assembly

See also: Sabbath

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Sabbath is the divinely ordained rhythm of one day in seven set apart for rest from ordinary labor and for worship of the Creator-Redeemer. Its ground is in creation: “God rested on the seventh day from all His work” (Gen 2:2), and He “blessed the seventh day and sanctified it” (Gen 2:3) — the pattern is pre-Mosaic and universal, not a Mosaic ceremony. The Fourth Commandment (Exod 20:8–11) formalizes the pattern as covenantal law: “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.” Six days are for labor; the seventh is “a Sabbath of the LORD your God.” The Deuteronomic formulation adds the redemptive ground: “you were a slave in Egypt” (Deut 5:15) — the Sabbath commemorates not only creation but redemption. Jesus's statement that “the Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27) does not abolish the institution but clarifies its purpose: the Sabbath is a gift, not a burden. Hebrews 4:9 declares that “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” — an eschatological Sabbath into which believers enter by faith. The Reformed tradition holds that the moral substance of the Fourth Commandment (one day in seven for rest and worship) continues in the New Covenant era and has been transferred from Saturday to Sunday by the authority of the risen Christ and apostolic practice — the Lord's Day (Rev 1:10; Acts 20:7; 1 Cor 16:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

SABBATH: the divinely ordained day of rest, grounded in creation (Gen 2:2–3) and commanded in the Decalogue (Exod 20:8); its moral substance continues in the New Covenant as the Lord's Day (Sunday), transferred by the resurrection and apostolic practice; eschatologically it anticipates the eternal rest of God's people (Heb 4:9).

expand to see more

SABBATH. n. [Heb. shabbat, from shabat, to rest.] A day of rest; the seventh day of the Jewish week, observed as a holy day from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday; in Christian usage, the first day of the week (Sunday, the Lord's Day), kept holy in commemoration of Christ's resurrection.

Webster (1828): “The day of rest from labor. It is applied also to the weekly day of rest and worship observed by Christians, being the first day of the week, which is called by way of eminence, the Christian Sabbath.” Webster's definition captures the Reformed position: the term migrates from the seventh to the first day without loss of meaning.

The Fourth Commandment's moral substance (one-in-seven rhythm of rest and worship) is distinguished from its ceremonial form (seventh day, Mosaic regulations) in the Reformed confessional tradition. The 1689 LBCF 22.7–8 states that the Sabbath was changed to the first day of the week by the authority of Christ and was to be perpetually observed as a day for the public and private worship of God.

Sabbatarian debates: Strict Sabbatarianism (Puritans, Westminster Confession 21.7–8) holds that the Lord's Day is wholly devoted to worship, excluding all secular employment and recreation except works of necessity and mercy. A softer Reformed position permits recreation after public worship. The dictionary's position follows the Westminster/1689 standard: the day is holy, and its primary use is public worship, private worship, acts of mercy, and holy rest.

Eschatological Sabbath (Heb 4:1–11): the weekly Sabbath is a type of the final rest into which believers enter by faith in Christ. The writer's argument moves from the creation rest of Gen 2:2, through the rest of Canaan, to a “rest that remains” for the people of God — entered now by faith and fully at the consummation.

Key Scripture

Gen 2:3 — "Then God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because in it He rested from all His work which God had created and made."

Exod 20:8 — "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy."

Mark 2:27 — "And He said to them, "The Sabbath was made for man — and not man for the Sabbath."

Heb 4:9 — "So there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God."

Modern Corruption

Antinomian evangelicalism treats the Sabbath as abolished with the ceremonial law and replaced by an undifferentiated use of all seven days; therapeutic culture turns the Lord's Day into a personal wellness day; both evacuate the commandment's creational, redemptive, and eschatological content.

expand to see more

The most common contemporary evangelical handling of the Fourth Commandment is a variant of the New Covenant theology position: the Sabbath was part of the Mosaic ceremonial law, and since Christ is the fulfillment of all ceremonial law, no day-specific obligation remains for the Christian. Colossians 2:16 (“let no man judge you in respect to a Sabbath day”) is the proof-text. The Reformed counter is threefold: (1) the Sabbath's ground is creation (Gen 2:3), not Sinai, which places it in the same category as the creational ordinances of marriage and labor, not the purely ceremonial Mosaic codes; (2) the Fourth Commandment is part of the moral law of the Decalogue, and the Decalogue's moral substance is not abolished but fulfilled and confirmed in Christ (Matt 5:17–18); (3) the New Testament evidence for Sunday assembly (Acts 20:7; 1 Cor 16:2; Rev 1:10) implies a continuing one-in-seven structure.

Therapeutic culture has produced a parallel corruption: the re-framing of Sunday as a personal mental-health rest day, organized around the individual's self-care needs rather than corporate worship and divine honor. “Practicing Sabbath” in this usage means intentional unplugging, nature walks, and creative leisure — none of which involves assembling with the body of Christ, hearing the preached Word, or celebrating the ordinances. This strips the Sabbath of its primary purposes (worship of the Creator-Redeemer and proclamation of the Gospel) and replaces them with the therapeutic self. The Sabbath is not primarily for the restoration of human productivity; it is for the hallowing of the living God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shabbat (rest, cessation from labor); the creation rest of Gen 2:2–3 as creational ordinance; the Decalogue's Fourth Commandment as moral law; transferral to the Lord's Day (Sunday) by apostolic authority; eschatological Sabbath-rest as the final inheritance of the redeemed.

expand to see more

Hebrew shabbat — to cease, to rest, to desist; the root implies intentional suspension of activity, not merely inactivity; the Sabbath is not the absence of labor but the deliberate consecration of a day — positive dedication to God, not merely negative abstinence from work

Creation Sabbath (Gen 2:2–3) — God rested on the seventh day not from fatigue but as a pattern for the week; the blessing and sanctification of the seventh day establishes Sabbath as a creational structure built into the rhythm of human existence before sin, before Moses, before the covenant at Sinai

Fourth Commandment (Exod 20:8–11; Deut 5:12–15) — the two versions of the Decalogue give two grounds: creation (Exodus) and redemption (Deuteronomy); the Sabbath therefore commemorates both God's creative work and His redemptive rescue from Egypt; in the New Covenant it commemorates the new creation (resurrection) and the new Exodus (redemption from sin)

Lord's Day (kuriake hēmera, Rev 1:10) — the New Testament designation for Sunday; the apostolic assemblies met on the first day (Acts 20:7); Paul organized the collection on the first day (1 Cor 16:2); the transfer from seventh to first day marks the new creation inaugurated by Christ's resurrection

Eschatological Sabbath (Heb 4:1–11) — the weekly Sabbath is typological: it points beyond itself to the final rest of the people of God, prefigured in Eden, foreshadowed in Canaan, and entered by faith in Christ now, fully at the consummation; “whoever has entered God's rest has also rested from his works as God did from his” (Heb 4:10)

Usage

"The pastor's practical task with the Lord's Day is to commend it as a gift rather than impose it as a legalistic burden. Jesus's statement that “the Sabbath was made for man” (Mark 2:27) frames the commandment in terms of benefit: a day of cessation from ordinary labor, corporate worship, and family rest is genuinely good for human creatures who are finite and embodied. The Reformed tradition's sabbatarianism has often struggled to commend this without producing Pharisaical restriction; the model is the family that genuinely looks forward to Sunday as the best day of the week."

"Corporate worship as the primary use of the Lord's Day is the Reformed standard that most challenges contemporary practice. When Sunday services become one optional leisure activity among others in the week, the communal and covenantal character of the day is lost. The 1689 LBCF 22.8 specifies: the whole day is to be kept holy to the Lord as public and private worship, duties of necessity and mercy, and holy rest. The sequence matters: public worship first, private devotion second, holy rest throughout, works of necessity when genuinely required."

"The Sabbath as protest against the 24/7 economy is a Reformed cultural contribution. In a world where productivity is the highest value and economic activity never ceases, the Sabbath-keeping congregation embodies a counter-cultural claim: creatures are not defined by their production; they are defined by their worship. The family that refuses Sunday commercial recreation and gathers for corporate worship is performing a public act of confession that the LORD is God and that His day belongs to Him."
